title: Does adding a nerve block reduce chronic pain after knee replacement?
official: Nerve Block for Chronic Pain After Knee replacement Surgery (BaCPAKS): a multi-centre, randomised, sham-controlled trial to investigate the clinical and cost effectiveness of adding an adductor canal block to standard perioperative approaches in primary elective knee joint replacement
summary:
Background and study aims
Knee replacement surgery is common. About 100,000 patients have this operation every year in the UK. Around half of patients report moderate or severe pain on the day after the operation (acute pain),which can lead to long-lasting pain (chronic pain). Patients with chronic pain have a poor quality of life,often leading to depression and anxiety. They may need to take time off work and have frequent medical visits. This has negative consequences for them and their families,and also for the NHS and society.
This study aims to find out if a treatment called adductor canal block (ACB) reduces pain after knee replacement. ACB is an injection of local anaesthetics to numb the thigh nerves. We think that patients receiving ACB will have reduced pain in the days after surgery (acute pain) and reduced pain in the months after surgery (chronic pain),compared to patients not receiving the ACB.

Who can participate?
People who are 18 years or older and need to have knee replacement surgery for any reason.

What does the study involve?
Half of the participants in the trial will receive an adductor canal block (ACB) at the start of their surgery, in addition to the standard pain relief given during the operation, which includes a local anaesthetic injected into the knee (LIA). The other half will receive a sham (pretend) version of the ACB at the same time point. The sham procedure is designed to look and feel similar to the real ACB but does not involve an injection or delivery of anaesthetic. Both the ACB and the sham will be carried out while participants are under general or spinal anaesthesia.
After the surgery, participants will complete several questionnaires to describe their pain and their recovery. The first questionnaire will be completed after consent but before your surgery. This may at a pre-operative visit, remotely, or on the day of the operation. Another questionnaire will be completed each day for up to three days after surgery, or until discharge (whichever comes first). After this, there will be additional questionnaires at 3, 6, and 12 months.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Those who take part in the trial will be helping to decide about the best treatment for people in the future. Participants will also be informed of the trial results, which may be of interest to them.
Additional risk from taking part in the trial is very small. In summary:
1. Those who require an injection may have bruising at the place where the needle is inserted.
2. There's a small chance of infection, but it's very unlikely. Sterile tools are used and participants’ skin is cleaned before the injection.
3. Some people might get a bruise or swelling called a haematoma. Ultrasound is used to help avoid blood vessels when guiding the needle.
4. There's a very small chance the needle might hurt a nerve, but this almost never happens. If it does, the nerve usually heals on its own in a few weeks, and long-term damage is almost never a concern.
5. Allergic reactions to the local anaesthetic are uncommon. 
6. Local anaesthetic toxicity is very rare. It can happen if too much of the medicine is given. The amount used in the trial is safe and within the proper limits.

Where is the study run from?
University of Birmingham (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
February 2027 to February 2030

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Health Technology Assessment Programme (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Ciro Morgese, BaCPAKS@trials.bham.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age ≥18 years
2. Primary elective unilateral knee replacement (KR) surgery for any indication, including both total (TKR) and uni-compartmental (uKR) knee replacements
Exclusion criteria:
1. Allergy to local anesthetics
2. Contraindications of  adductor canal block (ACB) including, but not limited to, infection at the site of injection,clotting abnormalities (INR>1.4 and/or platelets =<75 and/or on anticoagulants that have not been timely paused prior to surgery), anatomical abnormalities including, but not limited to, previous angioplasty and/or vascular surgery on the index limb 
3. Revision of KR surgery (i.e., non-primary KR surgery)
4. Planned epidural anaesthesia
5. Previous randomisation in the present trial for the other knee
6. Unable  or unwilling to comply with the study’s data collection requirements (including completing required questionnaires), or who are unable to provide informed consent
